item.title: Residents raise alarm over drug dealing in Lautoka informal settlements
item.description: Residents of informal settlements in Lautoka fear the growing presence of drug dealings is putting their safety at risk. Speaking to fijivillage News, a concerned resident says cases of glue sniffing and drug dealing are on the rise in Tavakubu Subdivision, however, the sale of drugs within Lautoka City has reduced over time due to increased Police patrols.
item.content:encoded:
Residents of informal settlements in Lautoka fear the growing presence of drug dealings is putting their safety at risk.

Speaking to fijivillage News, a concerned resident says cases of glue sniffing and drug dealing are on the rise in Tavakubu Subdivision, however, the sale of drugs within Lautoka City has reduced over time due to increased Police patrols.

He says there have been several occasions where people have come across used needles and syringes discarded in the area, raising fears for the safety of residents, particularly children.

Meanwhile, the resident had earlier told fijivillage News that some residents of Vunato Settlement claim drug dealing, brawls and other criminal activities are taking place in the Rifle Range informal settlement.

The resident says the Ministry has removed street dwellers from the city, describing it as a positive step as they are no longer exposed to danger.

The resident says while Police continue their efforts to track down drug dealers, it is equally important for every citizen to play their part by remaining vigilant and reporting suspicious activities.

item.title: Kadavu chiefs call for tighter jetty inspections to keep hard drugs out
item.description: Navitalai Naivalurua , Pita Toganivalu · 30/07/2026 The chiefs of Kadavu are calling on authorities to ensure that inspections are carried out on cargo and passengers arriving at the Vunisea and Kavala jetties to prevent hard drugs from entering the island.
item.content:encoded:
Navitalai Naivalurua , Pita Toganivalu · 30/07/2026

The chiefs of Kadavu are calling on authorities to ensure that inspections are carried out on cargo and passengers arriving at the Vunisea and Kavala jetties to prevent hard drugs from entering the island.

Speaking at the Kadavu Provincial Council meeting at the Civic Centre in Suva, one of the chiefs said hard drugs, including methamphetamine, have already made their way into Kadavu and are being used by young people.

He said cargo and passengers are routinely searched before departing from and upon arriving at the Suva Wharf on vessels travelling to and from Kadavu. However, he claimed that similar inspections are not conducted when cargo is unloaded or when passengers arrive at the jetties in Kadavu.

The chief called on Police to also conduct checks on passengers as they disembark from ships before they travel around the island.

He said action must be taken now to safeguard future generations.

Deputy Divisional Police Commander Central, Assistant Superintendent of Police (ASP) Isireli Ligairi, acknowledged the concern and said Police would take the issue into consideration.

While addressing the Council, ASP Ligairi told the chiefs they may have noticed that Operation Sasamaki is no longer being conducted as frequently because it has been suspended in Kadavu.

He said Police have now shifted their focus to maritime surveillance as part of the fight against drugs.

ASP Ligairi also said several laws are being reviewed, including the Police Act, the Illicit Drugs Control Act, and the Proceeds of Crime Act, to strengthen the country's legal framework in combating drugs.

He added that in the coming months, Police will also examine the income and assets of individuals to ensure their wealth has been acquired through legal means and is not the proceeds of marijuana cultivation or other criminal activity.

item.title: Fiji imports processed sugar for manufacturers- Tunabuna
item.description: Fiji imports processed white sugar for manufacturers such as Coca-Cola and other companies, while raw sugar for supermarkets is only imported when there is insufficient locally produced sugar. This was highlighted by Minister for Sugar Tomasi Tunabuna while speaking to fijivillage News, saying this is done particularly when production is low or after a natural disaster.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji imports processed white sugar for manufacturers such as Coca-Cola and other companies, while raw sugar for supermarkets is only imported when there is insufficient locally produced sugar.

This was highlighted by Minister for Sugar Tomasi Tunabuna while speaking to fijivillage News, saying this is done particularly when production is low or after a natural disaster.

Tunabuna says the Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC) has reported that it has some stock available for supermarkets.

He says Fiji normally imports raw sugar when there is insufficient sugar, especially when production is low or when the country experiences a natural disaster.

Insert:Tunabuna on sugar import 29th July.

The Minister says white sugar, icing sugar and other processed sugars are all imported and are not made from Fiji's brown sugar.

He explains that Fiji produces raw sugar, while processed sugars are imported at all times.

Providing an update on the crushing season, the Minister says the Lautoka and Labasa mills are operating at above 80 percent of their capacity, while the Ba Mill is operating at a little over 60 percent capacity, adding that production is now picking up.

Meanwhile, the Minister also highlights efforts to support diversification among sugarcane farmers.

He says last week he handed over a project to a farming community involved in sugarcane, which can also be used for cultivating other crops.

He says more than 30 rice harvesters have been provided over the past three weeks.

The Minister says they are also looking at increasing the fertiliser subsidy to include other crops so they can continue providing assistance to sugarcane farmers, allowing them to benefit from growing other crops, not just sugarcane.
